questions.text: How did the pain start — was it sudden and severe, or did it develop gradually over hours or days?
questions.purpose: Sudden severe testicular pain is the classic presentation of testicular torsion until proven otherwise
options: Chronic dull ache, weeks to months

questions.text: Did the pain start suddenly and is it severe enough that you cannot walk comfortably?
questions.purpose: Sudden severe pain strongly suggests testicular torsion — a urological emergency requiring immediate surgical assessment

questions.text: Have you noticed that the affected testicle appears higher than normal in the scrotum or is lying in an unusual position?
questions.purpose: A high-riding testicle with a horizontal lie is the clinical hallmark of testicular torsion

questions.text: Are you experiencing nausea or vomiting alongside the testicular pain?
questions.purpose: Nausea and vomiting accompany testicular torsion due to vagal stimulation from severe pain

questions.text: Do you have fever, urinary symptoms such as burning or frequency, or penile discharge alongside the pain?
questions.purpose: Fever with testicular pain suggests epididymo-orchitis, which requires a different pathway to torsion

questions.text: Have you had a recent scrotal injury or trauma?
questions.purpose: Identify traumatic aetiology which may still require urgent assessment for haematocele or rupture

questions.text: How old are you? Torsion is most common in males aged 12–25 years.
questions.purpose: Age 12–25 is the peak risk window for testicular torsion; this contextualises urgency
